title: A sealed event model
goal: By the end you can model payment events as a sealed hierarchy of data classes with value-class ids and amounts, parse untrusted fields into that model at the edge without throwing, and write operations as exhaustive `when` expressions that turn a new event type into a list of compile errors.

warmup.q: A log helper reads `when (event) { is PaymentCaptured -> "capture"; is PaymentRefunded -> "refund"; else -> "other" }`. A teammate adds `PaymentDisputed` to the sealed `PaymentEvent` interface and ships. What happens to disputes?
options: The build fails until the helper handles PaymentDisputed
They are logged as "other", and nothing tells anyone
The helper throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException at run time
Kotlin adds a branch for the new type automatically
warmup.why: The `else` branch matches anything, including types that didn't exist when it was written, so the compiler has nothing to report. Without the `else`, the same change is a compile error at this exact line. `NoWhenBranchMatchedException` only appears when a subtype compiled later reaches a `when` that was exhaustive when it was compiled.

sections.h: Parse at the edge, then trust the types

steps: Read the six messages in `EdgeDemo`'s `main`. For each, predict OK or REJECTED and the reason.
Run it.
Add a `declined` branch: a `PaymentDeclined(paymentId, reason: String)` data class (a record in Java), and a branch that reads the `reason` field. Run it again and check the count line.

code.title: EdgeDemo.kt

alt.title: EdgeDemoJava.java

try.expect: One message passes and five are rejected: `amountMinor is not a whole number: '12.50'`, `invalid payment id: '7781'`, `amount must not be negative: -500`, `missing field 'amountMinor'` and `unknown event type: 'declined'`. The id and the sign were refused by the constructors, not by the parser. With your `declined` branch the last line reads `2 accepted, 4 rejected`.

analogy: Think of the mailroom of a bank. Every envelope is opened there, once. A clerk either fills in the right typed form (a transfer, a complaint, a change of address) and sends it to a desk, or returns the letter with a note saying what was missing. The desks behind the mailroom only ever see forms, so they never squint at handwriting. The analogy breaks at one point: a good clerk may guess what a messy letter meant. The edge function must never guess. A missing amount is a rejection, not a zero.
in_your_world: In a Quarkus service the edge is usually the Kafka consumer: the deserializer hands you the record's JSON, `parseEvent` turns it into a `PaymentEvent`, and a `Rejected` goes to a dead-letter topic with the reason in a header, so the consumer can commit and move on. Webhooks from a card issuer, rows read back from an Oracle outbox table and signals into a Temporal workflow are edges too: each gets one parse function and nothing past it handles raw fields. When the producer team adds a new event type, deploy the consumers first: an old consumer rejects the unknown type at its edge and keeps running.
mistake: The common mistake is an edge that throws. `parseEvent` uses `!!`, `toLong()` and `require` directly, so a malformed message escapes as `NullPointerException` or `NumberFormatException`. In a Kafka consumer that exception fails the same record on every retry, and the partition stalls behind it. People write it because the throwing version is shorter and the happy-path test passes. The fix is to catch `IllegalArgumentException` once, around the whole parse, and return `Parsed.Rejected(e.message)`, so the caller decides where the bad message goes. Keep the checks themselves in the constructors.

compare.title: The event model in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Model.java (Java 21)

kotlin.title: Model.kt

compare.note: The shape is the same: sealed interfaces for the alternatives, final carriers for the leaves, validation in the constructor, and one exhaustive switch per operation. Three things differ. Kotlin's value classes compile to a `String` and a `long` wherever they're used as themselves, while Java's `PaymentId` and `Money` records are separate objects until value records arrive with Valhalla. Java names the subtypes in `permits` (or infers them within one file), while Kotlin requires them to share the package and module. And a data class's `copy()` runs `init`, so `captured.copy(amount = Money.ZERO)` throws; records have no `copy`. kotlinc writes the same `PermittedSubclasses` attribute that javac does, so Java code can switch exhaustively over this Kotlin model, which lesson 3 relies on.

worked.title: Add a new event type, end to end

steps.say: Chargebacks arrive: a cardholder disputes `pay_7781`, and the card scheme holds 19.99 until it's decided. First decide where the event goes. Money is held, not captured or refunded, so it is not a `MoneyMovement`. It's a direct subtype of `PaymentEvent`, with the same positive-amount rule as the others.

Compile before you write anything else. Every exhaustive `when` over `PaymentEvent` fails with `'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is PaymentDisputed' branch or an 'else' branch.` That list is the to-do list. Anything written against `MoneyMovement` still compiles, because its list of subtypes didn't change. Add the branch to `summary`:
steps.alt_code: case PaymentDisputed(var id, var amount) -> id + " disputed " + amount + " EUR";

steps.say: Now the edge. Its `when` is over a string, which can't be exhaustive, so it has an `else` and the compiler says nothing. A test has to do that job. The lab's `every event type has a summary line` test compares its samples with `PaymentEvent::class.sealedSubclasses`, so it fails until someone adds a disputed sample, and that reminds them to add the parser branch and its test:
steps.alt_code: case "disputed" -> new Ok(new PaymentDisputed(new PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields)));

steps.say: Last, the deploy order. Services that haven't been redeployed still parse raw fields with the old parser, so a `disputed` message lands in their `else` branch and becomes `Rejected("unknown event type: 'disputed'")` on the dead-letter topic. Nothing crashes. Deploy the consumers first, then the producer, and replay the dead letters if any arrived in between.

drill.title: Write the hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write the sealed hierarchy from memory: `PaymentEvent`, the sealed `MoneyMovement` and the four leaves (plain `String` ids and `Long` amounts are fine). Then write `movesMoney(e)` with no `else`, using one branch for `MoneyMovement`. Finally, add `PaymentDisputed` and say which of your functions must change.

recap: Stringly typed handlers each parse and check for themselves, so a bad message fails deep inside one of them after others have already acted on it.

A sealed interface closes the list of event types. Kotlin subtypes share its package and module; Java names them in `permits`. A sealed middle level such as `MoneyMovement` lets one branch stand for its leaves.
Write every operation as a `when` or `switch` with no `else`, so a new event type becomes a compile error at each place that must handle it.
Value classes make ids and amounts their own types at no cost where they're used as themselves, and their `init` blocks make every instance valid. One field only, so `Money` here is euro cents.
Parse once, at the edge, into the model. Return `Ok` or `Rejected`, never throw, and let the constructors make the checks. Behind the edge, trust the types.

quiz.q: From *Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check*: you move `PaymentRefunded` into a new package, `workbench.events.refunds`, in the same module. It still implements the sealed `MoneyMovement`. What happens?
options: It compiles: the same module is enough
kotlinc reports an error: a direct subtype of a sealed interface must be in the same package and module
It compiles with a warning, and `when` over MoneyMovement loses its exhaustiveness check
It compiles as long as the file is listed in `permits`
quiz.why: Kotlin's rule is the same package and the same module, with no `permits` clause at all. The closed list is what makes the `when` checkable, so the compiler refuses an inheritor elsewhere instead of quietly opening the hierarchy.

quiz.q: From *Value classes and what they compile to*: a `val recent: List<PaymentId>` holds 10,000 ids. What does the list hold at run time?
options: 10,000 `PaymentId` boxes, each wrapping a `String`
10,000 plain `String`s, because value classes are always erased
One shared `PaymentId` object
10,000 `PaymentId` objects, but only on JDK 25 and later
quiz.why: A value class is boxed whenever it's used as another type, and a generic type argument is one of those places. `List<PaymentId>` costs the same as `List<Long>` would: one object per element. The erasure to a plain `String` happens for fields, parameters and return values typed `PaymentId`.

quiz.q: `fun ledgerSign(e: MoneyMovement): Int = when (e) { is PaymentCaptured -> 1; is PaymentRefunded -> -1 }`. Someone adds `data class PaymentDisputed(...) : PaymentEvent`. Does `ledgerSign` still compile?
options: No: every `when` over the hierarchy must handle the new type
Only after adding an `else` branch
Yes, but it throws for disputes
Yes: the list of `MoneyMovement` subtypes didn't change
quiz.why: `ledgerSign` switches over `MoneyMovement`, and a dispute isn't one. Only `when`s over `PaymentEvent` itself get the new error. That is the benefit of a sealed middle level: code written against it is shielded from changes elsewhere in the tree. And a dispute can't reach `ledgerSign`, because the parameter type won't accept it.

quiz.q: From *Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla*: `parseEvent` receives `amountMinor = "-500"` for a refund. Which code should notice?
options: `parseEvent`, with its own `if (minor < 0)` check before building the event
The ledger handler, before it posts the refund
`Money`'s `init` block, and `parseEvent` turns its exception into `Rejected`
Nobody: a negative refund is a valid way to write a capture
quiz.why: The rule lives in the constructor, once, so every path that builds a `Money` obeys it. The parser only converts the refusal into a value. A second check in the parser drifts from the first, and a check in the handler means invalid events got past the edge.

quiz.q: From *State and Chain of Responsibility*: your service was compiled against model 1.4. At deploy time someone swaps in model 1.5, which adds `PaymentDisputed`, without recompiling the service. An in-process component built against 1.5 hands a dispute to the service's `summary`, which has no `else`. What happens?
options: `summary` returns an empty string
The JVM refuses to load `PaymentDisputed`
`summary` falls through to its last branch
`summary` throws `NoWhenBranchMatchedException`
quiz.why: Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time. For an exhaustive `when` with no `else`, kotlinc adds a hidden throw for the remainder: a subtype it never saw. Java's switch throws `MatchException` in the same situation. Events that arrive as raw fields avoid this, because the old parser rejects the unknown type at the edge.

flashcards.front: Why no `else` in a `when` over your own sealed type?
flashcards.back: Without it, a new subtype is a compile error at every `when` that must handle it. With it, the new subtype silently takes the `else` branch.

flashcards.front: What does a sealed middle level like `MoneyMovement` give you?
flashcards.back: One branch, `is MoneyMovement`, covers its leaves (captures and refunds), and code written against it doesn't break when siblings are added elsewhere.

flashcards.front: `@JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String)`: what is a `PaymentId` field at run time?
flashcards.back: A plain `String` field. It is boxed only when used as another type: generic, nullable, interface or `Any`.

flashcards.front: Why is `Money` here euro cents, with no currency?
flashcards.back: A JVM value class holds exactly one field. Amount plus currency would be a data class, one object per amount, and this service settles in euros only.

flashcards.front: What does the edge function return for a malformed message?
flashcards.back: `Parsed.Rejected(reason)`, never an exception. The caller routes it: dead-letter topic, log line, metric.

flashcards.front: Where does `parseEvent` check that a payment id is well formed?
flashcards.back: It doesn't. It calls `PaymentId(raw)`, whose `init` checks, and turns the `IllegalArgumentException` into `Rejected`.

flashcards.front: An old service gets a message of a new event type as raw fields. What happens?
flashcards.back: Its parser's `else` branch returns `Rejected("unknown event type")`. Nothing crashes, so deploy consumers before producers.

terms.plain: A type whose list of direct subtypes is closed and known to the compiler.
A `when` or `switch` with a branch for every possible subtype and no `else`, checked at compile time.
A one-field wrapper that is its own type in Kotlin and compiles to its field where it can.
The one place where raw input from outside the service becomes model values, or is refused.
A Kafka topic that holds messages a consumer refused, with the reason, so they can be inspected or replayed.
The cases an exhaustive switch can still meet at run time: null, and subtypes compiled after it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why handlers take a `PaymentCaptured` instead of the Kafka record's `Map<String, String>`: "the map has everything, and it's one less type to maintain." Explain what the sealed model and the edge buy you, using a bug you could get with the map.
explain_back.answer: With the map, every handler parses and validates for itself. A capture with amount "12.50" throws inside the ledger after the audit handler already logged it, and a typo like "capture" silently never matches. The model closes the list of event types, so a `when` without `else` lists every place that must change when a type is added. Value classes make a swapped id and amount a compile error, and their constructors make every instance valid. The edge parses each record once and returns `Ok` or `Rejected`, so a bad message goes to the dead-letter topic before any handler acts. Behind it, a handler that takes a `PaymentCaptured` knows it has a valid id and a positive amount. The extra types cost a few lines; they remove a whole class of 2 a.m. bugs.

deeper.body:
Three questions come up once a model like this is in production.

How do events evolve? Adding a field with a default is safe for consumers that parse at the edge: old messages lack the field and get the default. Renaming a type or a field is not. Keep the old name in the parser for as long as old messages can arrive, and map it to the new type there, so the model itself never carries the history. If you serialize the model with kotlinx.serialization, as *Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization* showed, pin each type's name with `@SerialName` for the same reason.

Should the edge return `Either` instead of a sealed `Parsed`? `Either<String, PaymentEvent>` from *Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus* works, and composes with `map` and `flatMap`. A dedicated `Parsed` reads better at the call site (`is Parsed.Rejected`) and leaves room for a third case later, such as `Ignored` for event types a service deliberately doesn't handle. Kotlin's `Result<T>` is the wrong fit: its failure side is a `Throwable`, and a rejection is not an exception.

What about the database? Rows you read back are untrusted input too. A column holding `'captured'` and a nullable `amount_minor` is a raw map with a schema, and a migration or a manual fix can break it. Read rows through the same kind of edge function, or reuse `parseEvent` by turning each row into its field map.

Java has one tool here that Kotlin lacks: since JDK 21 a pattern switch can take `case null` explicitly, while Kotlin rules out null at compile time by declaring the parameter non-nullable. Both end up with the same guarantee behind the edge.
